Algebra 1 | Quarter 2 | Unit 3: Linear Relationships

Mapping the Bike Park

Where on the map is the jump line?

Duration
50 minutes
Grade level
Grades 8–9
Topic
Coordinate Plane
Standards
6.NS.C.8, 5.G.A.2, HSN-Q.A.1

Students use a coordinate grid to map a bike park, name points and quadrants, and read graphs whose two axes use different scales, the way a trail profile does.

2Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  • Identify the x-axis, y-axis, origin and the four quadrants.
  • Read and write the coordinates of a point as an ordered pair (x, y).
  • Tell which quadrant a point is in from the signs of its coordinates.
  • Read a graph whose axes use different scales, such as a trail profile.

3Essential question

How can two numbers describe exactly where something is, on a map or on a graph?

5MTB connection

Trail maps and trail profiles are coordinate graphs. A park map uses x and y for east and north; an elevation profile uses x for distance and y for elevation. Riders read both before every new trail.

Profile graphs on apps like Strava and Trailforks stretch the vertical scale so small hills are visible. Learning to read the scale on each axis is what keeps a rider from panicking at a climb that only looks like a wall.

The mathOn the trail
OriginThe trailhead or start line
Ordered pairA feature’s location, or (distance, elevation) on a profile
Negative coordinatesWest or south of the trailhead
Different axis scalesAn elevation profile that exaggerates steepness

7MTB activity

MTB Classroom Activity

Bike Park Grid Map

Use coordinates to locate, plot and describe features of a bike park relative to the trailhead.

You’ll need: The bike park map projected or printed (the figure in the Mathematical foundation, with labels covered); Grid paper; Colored pencils
